title: Ibn Khaldun Writes the Muqaddimah, a Theory of How Dynasties Rise and Fall
dek: In retreat at a fortress in the hills of western Algeria, a North African statesman drafts an introduction to world history that explains why ruling houses rise and fall.
body: Its idea of asabiyyah, the cohesion that lets a group seize power and then fades in luxury, still shapes how people explain the rise and fall of states.

panels.label: His Modern Admirers Said
panels.text: Arnold Toynbee called the Muqaddimah "the greatest work of its kind", and readers from Ernest Gellner to Ronald Reagan said it anticipated modern social science, political theory and economics.

panels.label: His Biographer Said
panels.text: Robert Irwin said Ibn Khaldun was a 14th-century Muslim jurist, almost certainly a Sufi, who believed sorcery was real, and that modern admirers had remade him in their own image.

panels.label: The Stakes
panels.text: Both camps say they read him as he was; at stake is whose authority the Muqaddimah lends: a secular science of power seeking an ancestor, or the Islamic learning that produced it.
